name: APT5
affiliation_detail:
Mandiant characterizes APT5 as "a large threat group that consists of several subgroups, often with distinct tactics and infrastructure," (Mandiant, n.d.)
The NSA attributed the 2022 Citrix ADC zero-day exploitation to APT5 in a named advisory. (NSA, 2022)
No specific MSS bureau, PLA unit, or contractor has been publicly identified.
Mandiant notes that UNC2630's targeting "generally line up with collection requirements for the Chinese government." (Mandiant, 2021) The UNC2630 linkage to APT5 is assessed rather than definitive. Mandiant stated: "Although we are not able to definitively connect UNC2630 to APT5, or any other existing APT group, a trusted third party has uncovered evidence connecting this activity to historic campaigns which Mandiant tracks as Chinese espionage actor APT5." (Mandiant, 2021)
description:
APT5 is a China-based cyber espionage actor active since at least 2007, primarily targeting the telecommunications, aerospace, and defense industries across the United States, Europe, and Asia. Mandiant characterizes it as "a large threat group that consists of several subgroups, often with distinct tactics and infrastructure." (Mandiant, n.d.)
The group is distinguished by its focus on compromising network infrastructure devices — VPN appliances, routers, application delivery controllers — and modifying their underlying software to maintain persistent access while bypassing authentication controls. As early as 2014, Mandiant observed APT5 making unauthorized code modifications to files in embedded operating systems of technology platforms. In 2015, APT5 compromised a U.S. telecommunications organization and "downloaded and modified some of the router images related to the company's network routers." (Mandiant, n.d.)
In April 2021, Mandiant documented APT5 (tracked as UNC2630) exploiting a zero-day in Pulse Secure VPN appliances to target U.S. defense industrial base networks. The group deployed 16 distinct malware families specifically designed for Pulse Secure devices. CISA issued an emergency directive requiring all federal agencies to assess their Pulse Secure deployments. (Mandiant, 2021; CISA, 2021)
In December 2022, the NSA published a named advisory attributing active exploitation of a Citrix ADC zero-day to APT5. The vulnerability allowed unauthenticated remote code execution on Citrix Application Delivery Controller and Gateway devices. (NSA, 2022) APT5 has also been documented using ORB (Operational Relay Box) networks — specifically the SPACEHOP infrastructure — for network reconnaissance and exploit delivery, raising the cost of attribution for defenders. (Mandiant, 2024)

campaigns.name: Pulse Secure VPN Zero-Day Exploitation (UNC2630)
campaigns.description: Mandiant documented UNC2630 (assessed as APT5) exploiting a zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2021-22893) in Pulse Secure VPN appliances to target U.S. defense industrial base networks beginning August 2020. The group deployed 16 malware families designed specifically for Pulse Secure, including SLOWPULSE (which bypasses LDAP and RADIUS 2FA), ATRIUM, PACEMAKER, and RADIALPULSE. CISA issued Emergency Directive 21-03 requiring all federal agencies to assess their Pulse Secure environments. Mandiant noted "these actors display an unusual sensitivity to publicity" after observing UNC2630 rapidly remove backdoors from dozens of devices around the time of public disclosure. (Mandiant, 2021)

campaigns.name: Citrix ADC Zero-Day Exploitation (CVE-2022-27518)
campaigns.description: The NSA published a named advisory attributing active exploitation of a critical Citrix ADC zero-day (CVE-2022-27518, CVSS 9.8) to APT5. The vulnerability allowed unauthenticated remote code execution on Citrix Application Delivery Controller and Gateway devices configured with SAML SP or IdP. APT5 modified legitimate binaries for persistence, requiring investigation beyond patching. CISA added the CVE to the KEV catalog on December 13, 2022. (NSA, 2022; Citrix, 2022)

campaigns.name: Telecom and Router Infrastructure Compromise (2014–2015)
campaigns.description: Mandiant documented APT5 making unauthorized code modifications to files in the embedded operating system of a technology platform as early as 2014. In 2015, APT5 compromised a U.S. telecommunications organization and downloaded and modified router images. During the same period, APT5 stole military technology files from a South Asian defense organization, including product specifications, procurement bids, and documents on unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). (Mandiant, n.d.)
